lesson.title: The Lowest It Gets: The Minimum Value of a Parabola
lesson.summary: When a parabola opens upward, its vertex sits lower than every other point on the curve, and the vertex's y-coordinate is called the function's minimum value.
lesson.body:
This is the mirror image of the last section: when a is positive, a parabola opens upward, and the vertex becomes the single lowest point on the graph. The y-coordinate of that vertex is the minimum value of the function, no input produces a smaller output.

This pattern is exactly what you want when a real quantity, like cost, has a low point you are trying to find. Suppose the cost in dollars to produce x hundred units of some item is modeled by C(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 25. Here a = 2, which is positive, so the parabola opens upward and a minimum cost exists, business questions like how many units should be produced to minimize cost are really just asking you to find a vertex.

Use the same formula as always: x = -b/(2a). With a = 2 and b = -12, x = -(-12)/(2·2) = 12/4 = 3. Substitute back to find the minimum cost itself: C(3) = 2(3)^2 - 12(3) + 25 = 2(9) - 36 + 25 = 18 - 36 + 25 = 7. So the minimum cost is $7, in whatever hundreds-of-units and dollar scale the problem used, occurring when x = 3.

Check it against nearby values to confirm: C(2) = 2(4) - 24 + 25 = 8 - 24 + 25 = 9, and C(4) = 2(16) - 48 + 25 = 32 - 48 + 25 = 9. Both are larger than 7, and both come from x-values 1 unit on either side of x = 3, the axis of symmetry, matching that reflected pattern again. Whether a vertex represents a maximum or a minimum always comes down to that one sign check on a: opening upward bounds the function from below, opening downward bounds it from above.
